n: Jeremiah’s first recorded sermon begins. It’s like a lawsuit from God against His unfaithful people.
God remembers Israel’s early devotion—like a young bride’s love—when she followed Him through the barren desert after the Exodus. The covenant is pictured as a marriage.

f.g: Your love as a bride (espousals = betrothal or wedding).

f.w: a land that was not sown

n: Israel was holy to the Lord, like the firstfruits of a harvest set apart for Him. Anyone who “ate” this sacred portion was guilty and would suffer.

f.g: The first and best of the harvest, which belonged to God and was forbidden to others.

n: Hear the Lord’s word, all Israel’s families.
What fault did your ancestors find in Me that they wandered so far, chasing worthless idols and becoming worthless themselves? We become like what we worship.

f.w: walked after vanity, and are become vain
f.g: Vanity = Hebrew hevel, “breath, vapor”—emptiness. Followed emptiness and became empty.

n: They never even asked, “Where is the Lord who brought us out of Egypt and guided us through that terrible desert?” They forgot their history.
God brought them into a fruitful land, but they polluted it and made His inheritance disgusting.
Every kind of leader failed: priests didn’t seek God, teachers of the law didn’t know Him, rulers rebelled, and prophets spoke for Baal.

f.g: The Canaanite storm and fertility god.

n: So God will bring charges against them—and against their grandchildren.

f.g: Bring a legal case, contend in court.

n: Go west to the islands of Cyprus or east to the Arabian tribes of Kedar and look carefully: has anything like this ever happened?
No nation ever traded its gods—even though they aren’t real gods. Yet Israel traded its glorious God for worthless things.
Be appalled, O heavens! Shudder and be horrified! God calls creation to witness this betrayal.

A famous image: My people did two wrongs. They abandoned Me, the spring of living water, and dug cracked cisterns that can’t hold water. Why trade a fresh, flowing spring for stale water in a leaking tank?

f.g: Living water = fresh, flowing spring water.
Plastered pits dug in rock to store rainwater; if cracked, they leaked.

n: Is Israel a slave by birth? Why has he become plunder?

f.g: A slave born in his master’s household.

n: Lions (foreign armies) have roared over him, wasted his land, and burned his cities.
Even Egyptians from Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved Israel’s head—humiliated it. King Josiah later died fighting Egypt.

f.g: Memphis, a major city of Egypt.

f.w: broken the crown of thy head
f.g: Shaved or cracked your skull—a humiliation.

n: Haven’t you brought this on yourself by abandoning the Lord when He was leading you?
Why go to Egypt to drink from the Nile, or to Assyria to drink from the Euphrates? Judah kept looking to foreign powers for security instead of God.
Your own wickedness will punish you. Learn how bitter it is to abandon the Lord. Sin often carries its own consequences.

f.w: Thine own wickedness shall correct thee

n: God broke Israel’s yoke of slavery long ago, and they promised to serve Him—yet on every high hill and under every green tree they committed spiritual adultery with idols.

f.g: A prophetic metaphor for worshipping other gods—covenant unfaithfulness.

n: God planted Israel as a choice vine from pure stock. How did it become a wild, corrupt vine? Compare Isaiah’s song of the vineyard and Zenos’s allegory of the olive tree.
No amount of washing with lye and soap will remove the stain of their guilt. Only God can cleanse sin.

f.g: Natron or lye, a mineral used as soap.

f.w: thine iniquity is marked before me

n: How can you claim you haven’t worshipped Baals? Look at what you did in the valley (likely the Valley of Hinnom). You’re like a restless young camel running in every direction.

f.g: Plural of Baal—local versions of the god.

f.w: see thy way in the valley

n: Like a wild donkey in heat sniffing the wind, she can’t be restrained; her pursuers don’t even have to try. Judah eagerly chases idols.
Don’t run your feet bare and your throat dry chasing idols! But Judah says, “It’s no use—I love foreign gods and I’ll follow them.”
Like a thief caught in the act, Israel—kings, princes, priests, and prophets—will be ashamed.
They call a block of wood “my father” and a stone “my mother,” turning their backs on God—yet in trouble they cry, “Save us!” People often remember God only in crisis.

f.g: Block of wood—an idol or wooden pole.

f.w: in the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us

n: Where are the gods you made? Let them save you! Judah has as many gods as it has cities.

f.w: according to the number of thy cities are thy gods

n: Why argue with Me? You have all rebelled.
God disciplined them, but they didn’t learn. They killed their own prophets like a ravaging lion.

f.w: your own sword hath devoured your prophets

n: Have I been a barren desert or a dark land to Israel? Why do they say, “We’re free; we won’t come to You anymore”?

f.g: We roam freely; we answer to no one.

n: Does a bride forget her jewelry or wedding sash? Yet My people have forgotten Me for countless days.
You’re so skilled at chasing lovers that even the wicked can learn from you.
Your clothing is stained with the blood of innocent poor people—not hidden away, but out in the open.

f.w: the blood of the souls of the poor innocents

n: Yet you insist, “I’m innocent; surely His anger has passed.” God will judge precisely because you say you haven’t sinned. Denial blocks repentance.
Why do you keep changing course, running from one ally to another? Egypt will disappoint you just as Assyria did.
You’ll leave Egypt with your hands on your head—a sign of grief and shame—because the Lord has rejected the ones you trusted.

f.g: A gesture of mourning or disgrace.
